script.text: Two A.I. labs say they broke a famous computing rule. Can anyone confirm it?

The Exponential Time Hypothesis, from the late nineteen nineties, says a hard puzzle called three-SAT has no fast shortcut. Many results in computer science rest on it. On October twenty-sixth, OpenAI said its model found a faster method.

Science reported that Anthropic made a similar claim. Both are company claims in papers that are not peer-reviewed. OpenAI says it also checked its proof with Lean, software that verifies every logical step.

Now outside experts are checking. The hypothesis's original authors, including M.I.T.'s Ryan Williams, are helping organize an open review. Holger Dell, who was not involved, called it a major breakthrough. Even so, the famous P versus N.P. question stays open.
Will outside experts confirm the proof? Yes or no?

upload.title: OpenAI Says Its A.I. Broke a Core Computing Rule #shorts
upload.description:
OpenAI says an internal model refuted the Exponential Time Hypothesis, a widely used assumption about how hard the 3-SAT puzzle is. Science reports that Anthropic made a similar claim. Both are company claims in papers that are not yet peer-reviewed; the hypothesis's original authors are helping organize an open review.

Sources: Science, The Washington Times, The Next Web, OpenAI statement and preprint (Oct 26), Forklog. All results are company claims, not yet independently confirmed.
